chunks: What RAM is (SRAM vs DRAM). The question: What is RAM?
RAM is working memory that you can both read and write, where any location takes about the same time to reach. There are two main kinds.
SRAM stores each bit in a small circuit that holds its value while power is on.
It is fast but takes a lot of space, so it is used for caches (small, fast memories next to the processor). DRAM stores each bit as a tiny electric charge.
It is smaller and cheaper, so it is used for main memory, but the charge leaks away and must be topped up.
SRAM is a light switch. Once you set it on or off, it stays there. DRAM is a bucket with a slow leak: a full bucket means 1 and an empty one means 0.
You must refill the full buckets every so often, before they run dry. Checking a DRAM bucket means pouring it out to see what was in it, so it is refilled after each read.

Two cross-coupled inverters (the outputs Q and QB feed each other's input) hold one bit; the word line WL turns on both access NMOS transistors so the bit-line pair BL/BLB can read or overwrite the latch.
Volatile: loses its contents when power is removed. Transistor: a tiny electrically controlled switch.
Capacitor: a tiny part that stores electric charge, like a very small bucket.
Refresh: reading and rewriting every DRAM row (one line of cells) regularly, before its charge leaks away.
Sense amplifier: a circuit that detects a tiny voltage change and boosts it to a clear 0 or 1.
Compare 1 MB of each. 1 MB is 8,388,608 bits. An SRAM cell uses 6 transistors, so the array needs about 50 million transistors.
A DRAM cell uses 1 transistor and 1 capacitor, so it needs about 8. 4 million of each. That is why DRAM packs far more bits into the same area.
The price is refresh, which happens every 64 milliseconds or so, and slower access. That is the whole idea.
"RAM is random-access, read/write, normally volatile working memory. There are two main types.
SRAM stores a bit in a six-transistor latch, so it's fast and needs no refresh but takes a lot of area; it's used for caches and on-chip RAM.

DRAM stores a bit as charge on a capacitor with one access transistor, so it's dense and cheap but slower, reads are destructive, and the charge leaks, so rows must be refreshed every tens of milliseconds.
Hence SRAM for small fast levels and DRAM for large main memory."
